_comment: PostgreSQL provider as the WRITE-PATH ORACLE -- feature 9 (OWNER-DECISIONS.md
Batch 5; feature doc 009-postgresql-provider.md PG-DEC-01). PostgreSQL is
Tina4's production-grade reference engine: it is the adapter that most
exercises the write contract -- native RETURNING, a real generated last-id,
transactions, exact affected counts -- and the model the other providers are
measured against.
PG-DEC-01: make the adapter-contract test assert real BEHAVIOUR (not just
method presence) with PostgreSQL as the reference model, in all four. The old
adapter-contract runners proved a method EXISTED; these invariants prove the
write path BEHAVES, on a REAL PostgreSQL, no mocks.
SCOPE: this fixture pins exactly what PostgreSQL-as-the-oracle needs -- the
write-path behaviours below. The full 14-method adapter interface redesign
(feature 3, ADR-0044, adapter_contract.json) is a separate, larger piece of
work and its runners remain OWED; nothing here depends on it.
NO MOCKS. Every case drives the lab's real PostgreSQL :55432 (tina4/tina4)
through the public Database facade -> the PostgreSQLAdapter, and reads durable
state back on a SECOND, FRESH connection where durability is the property
under test. The oracle table is a real SERIAL-key table so the generated
last-id comes from PostgreSQL's own sequence via RETURNING, not a guess; each
case first TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY so the generated ids are deterministic.
The behaviours, each an invariant proven in all four:
1. pg-insert-returning-last-id  -- an insert returns a DatabaseResult whose
last_id is the RETURNING-generated key and whose affected count is 1; a
second insert returns the NEXT generated id, never a stale earlier one.
2. pg-write-affected-count      -- update/delete report the EXACT number of
rows they touched, and report last_id null (last_id is insert-only).
3. pg-filterless-write-guard    -- an update with neither a filter nor a
primary key, and a delete with no filter, RAISE and change nothing
(verified on a fresh connection); truncate() is the explicit empty.
4. pg-executemany-atomicity     -- a standalone execute_many owns ONE
transaction: a mid-batch failure rolls the whole batch back, so a FRESH
connection sees ZERO rows; empty input is a zero-row no-op that opens no
transaction.
5. pg-fetch-shape               -- fetch returns a native list of row maps
(records), keyed by the selected columns with each value preserved in the
host language's own idiom (Python/Ruby/Node get a native int for an
INTEGER column; PHP's ext-pgsql returns the value as a string -- native
for that driver -- so the cross-language gate is value-correctness + the
list-of-maps shape, NOT one language's type map, per the write-path
contract's own note that type mapping varies by engine); fetch_one returns
one native record or null.
Mutation-proved (all four): make execute_many commit each row instead of
owning one transaction and 'execute many mid batch failure rolls back on a
fresh connection' goes RED (the first row survives on the fresh connection);
drop the filterless-write guard and the guard cases go RED (rows change / a
whole table empties); return a bare affected-count instead of a DatabaseResult
and the last-id / affected-count cases go RED. Restoring each returns to green.
Each invariant names a REAL suite file per framework carrying the SAME case
names in each language's own idiom, which scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py
normalises and matches.
Env contract (identical to the write-path runner): TINA4_TEST_PG_URL /
TINA4_TEST_PG_USERNAME / TINA4_TEST_PG_PASSWORD, falling back to the shared
TINA4_TEST_WRITE_PATH_URL / _USERNAME / _PASSWORD, then TINA4_DATABASE_*.
feature: 9 - PostgreSQL provider as the write-path oracle (PG-DEC-01: the adapter-contract test asserts write-path BEHAVIOUR against a real PostgreSQL, all four)

invariants.rule: On a real PostgreSQL, db.insert() returns a DatabaseResult whose last_id is the key PostgreSQL generated for that row via native RETURNING (not a guessed or probed value), whose affected_rows is 1, and a second insert returns the NEXT generated id -- never the earlier row's id. Identical in all four (Python Database.insert -> PostgreSQLAdapter.execute; PHP Database::insert -> PostgresAdapter; Ruby Database#insert -> PostgresDriver; Node Database.insert -> PostgresAdapter).
invariants.why: PostgreSQL is the oracle for the last-insert-id contract because RETURNING gives the TRUE generated key on the same statement and connection as the write. A stale or wrong last_id silently corrupts the next row a caller writes keyed on it. Proven on a real SERIAL-key table with RESTART IDENTITY so the generated id is deterministic (first insert -> 1, second -> 2), no mocks.
cases: insert returns the returning generated last id
insert reports affected rows of one
a second insert returns the next generated id not a stale one

invariants.rule: On a real PostgreSQL, db.update() and db.delete() return a DatabaseResult whose affected_rows is EXACTLY the number of rows the write touched (never the number of statements, never a bare boolean), and whose last_id is null because last_id is insert-only. Identical in all four.
invariants.why: A write that reports the wrong affected count lets a caller believe a no-op succeeded or a multi-row write hit one row. PostgreSQL reports an exact rowcount, so it is the oracle for the affected-count contract. Proven on a real table with a known seed, no mocks: an update whose filter matches two of three rows reports 2, a delete of one row reports 1.
cases: update reports the exact number of rows changed
update reports a null last id
delete reports the exact number of rows removed

invariants.rule: On a real PostgreSQL, an update with neither an explicit filter nor a primary key in its data RAISES rather than rewriting every row, and a delete with no filter RAISES rather than emptying the table; in both cases the table is UNCHANGED, verified by reading every row back on a fresh connection. truncate() is the explicit, separate whole-table empty. Identical in all four.
invariants.why: The single most dangerous write-path bug is a filterless UPDATE/DELETE that silently touches every row and reports success. PostgreSQL makes the data-loss real, so the guard is proven where it matters. Proven on a real seeded table, no mocks: after the raise, a fresh connection still sees exactly the seeded rows.
cases: update without a filter or primary key raises and changes nothing
delete without a filter raises and removes nothing

invariants.rule: On a real PostgreSQL, a standalone db.execute_many() owns ONE transaction: it begins once, runs every parameter set, and commits once; a mid-batch failure rolls the WHOLE batch back so a FRESH connection sees ZERO rows from the batch, and the call raises. Empty input is a successful zero-row no-op that opens no transaction and writes nothing. Identical in all four.
invariants.why: executeMany owns work that cannot be reconstructed above the adapter -- one physical connection, transaction ownership, rollback and affected-row accounting. If it committed each row instead of owning one transaction, a batch that fails partway would leave the earlier rows durable -- a silent partial write. PostgreSQL's real transaction is the oracle. Proven no-mocks by forcing a UNIQUE violation on the second set (the first set already executed within the batch) and reading COUNT(*) = 0 on a fresh connection. Mutation-proved: commit each row instead of owning the transaction and the first row survives on the fresh connection -> RED.
cases: execute many mid batch failure rolls back on a fresh connection
execute many empty input is a zero row no op

invariants.rule: On a real PostgreSQL, db.fetch() returns a DatabaseResult whose records are a native list of row maps keyed by the selected columns with each value preserved (compared in the host language's idiom: Python/Ruby/Node yield a native int for an INTEGER column, PHP's ext-pgsql yields the same value as a string -- native for that driver), and db.fetch_one() returns exactly one native record for a match or null for no match. The cross-language gate is the list-of-maps shape + value-correctness + the one-or-null result, not a single language's type map (the write-path contract already records that INTEGER type mapping varies by engine). Identical in all four.
invariants.why: The read contract is that the caller gets a native list of row maps with values preserved, not a scalar, a stringified blob, or an envelope-only result; PostgreSQL's typed protocol is the oracle. A fetch that loses the rows, or a fetch_one that returns an empty envelope instead of null, breaks every consumer downstream. Proven no-mocks against a real seeded table.
cases: fetch returns a native list of rows with native types
fetch one returns a single native record
fetch one with no match returns null
